ch4-1.12.title: Problem 1.12 — Do Canadian households spend too much?
ch4-1.12.body: Household debt is becoming an ever more serious concern for the Canadian economy. By the end of September 2024, Canadians’ debt-to-disposable-income ratio was 173.1 percent, meaning the average Canadian was carrying debt equal to more than 1.7 times their after-tax income. In 2000 the ratio was much lower, at 110 percent. Economists identify current debt as a risk to future growth, because Canadians will have to cut debt and build up savings.

questions.prompt: Why in microeconomics do we measure production in terms of quantity, but in macroeconomics we measure production in terms of market value?

options.text: Macroeconomics must add up very different goods and services (cars, haircuts, food) into one total, which needs a common unit; market value (price × quantity) provides it
Macroeconomics studies only prices, so quantities are irrelevant
Quantities of goods cannot be measured for the economy as a whole
Market values are unaffected by inflation, so they give a more accurate measure of output

questions.explanation: You cannot meaningfully add cars to haircuts to bushels of wheat. In microeconomics we study one good at a time, so units work. For the whole economy we need a **common unit, and market value in dollars is that unit**. (Market values do move with prices, which is why real GDP is introduced later.)

questions.prompt: If Statistics Canada added up the values of every good and service sold during the year, would the total be larger or smaller than GDP?

options.text: Smaller, because GDP also includes the value of imported goods
Larger, because it would count intermediate goods repeatedly and also resales of used goods
Exactly the same, because GDP is the total value of everything sold
Smaller, because sales leave out government purchases that GDP includes

questions.explanation: GDP counts only **final** goods and services produced in the period. Summing every sale would count intermediate goods (e.g. the wheat, then the flour, then the bread) multiple times, and would add resales of used goods produced earlier. The total would therefore be **larger** than GDP.

questions.prompt: In the circular flow of income, why must the value of total production in an economy equal the value of total income?

options.text: Because the government sets income equal to production through its taxes and transfers
Because households spend exactly all of their income on domestically produced goods
Every dollar spent on final goods becomes revenue for firms, and firms pay all of that revenue out as wages, rent, interest and profit to the owners of the factors of production
Because prices adjust automatically until production equals income in each market

questions.explanation: The value of what is produced equals what is spent on it (revenue to firms). Firms in turn pay out **all** of that revenue as income to households: wages, rent, interest, and profit to the owners. So **total production = total spending = total income**. This is an accounting identity; it does not require that households spend all their income or that government acts.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are major categories of expenditure in GDP (national-accounts version)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Final consumption
Government transfer payments
Gross fixed capital formation
Purchases of intermediate goods
Investment in inventories
Net exports

questions.explanation: The four expenditure categories are **final consumption** (households, government and non-profits), **gross fixed capital formation** (fixed assets such as buildings and machinery), **investment in inventories**, and **net exports**. Transfer payments are not purchases of newly produced output, and intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting.

questions.prompt: Which equation relates GDP to the four expenditure categories?

options.text: GDP = final consumption + saving + taxes + (exports − imports)
GDP = final consumption + gross fixed capital formation + transfer payments + (exports + imports)
GDP = final consumption + intermediate goods + investment in inventories + imports
GDP = final consumption + gross fixed capital formation + investment in inventories + (exports − imports)

questions.explanation: GDP is total spending on final goods and services produced domestically: consumption, plus investment (fixed capital and inventories), plus **net exports = exports − imports**. Imports are subtracted because they are included in spending but were not produced in Canada. (In the simplified macro-model version this is **Y = C + I + G + Nx**.)

questions.prompt: What is meant by a firm’s “value added”?

options.text: The market value the firm adds to a product: its sales revenue minus what it pays for intermediate goods and services
The firm’s total revenue from selling the finished product
The firm’s profit after paying all wages, rent and interest
The tax the government collects on the firm’s final sale

questions.explanation: Value added = **sale price of the output − payments for intermediate goods**. It is larger than profit, because it also includes the wages, rent and interest the firm pays. Summing value added across every stage of production gives the final selling price, and hence GDP.

questions.prompt: A student says: “It doesn’t make sense that intermediate goods are not counted in GDP. A computer chip is an intermediate good, and without it a PC won’t work. So why don’t we count the computer chip in GDP?” What is the best reply?

options.text: Chips are not valuable enough to be counted in a country’s output
The chip’s value is already included in the price of the final PC; counting it separately as well would double count it
GDP counts only goods bought by consumers, never goods bought by firms
Chips are produced in other countries, so they can never be in Canadian GDP

questions.explanation: GDP counts the **final** good only. The price of the PC already reflects the chip, so adding the chip’s sale as well would **double count** it. (Firms do buy final goods, such as machinery, and those do count; only inputs used up in producing other goods are excluded.)

questions.prompt: Part (a): “The purchase of wheat from a wheat farmer by a bakery” is the purchase of a final good.
questions.explanation: The bakery uses the wheat as an input to make bread, so it is an **intermediate good**; the bread is the final good.

questions.prompt: Part (b): “The purchase of a frigate by the federal government” is the purchase of a final good.
questions.explanation: The government is the final user of the frigate, so it is a **final good** (government spending).

questions.prompt: Part (c): “The purchase of a French wine by a Canadian consumer” is the purchase of a final good.
questions.explanation: The consumer is the final user, so it is a final good. Because it is an **import**, it is added to consumption but subtracted again in net exports, so it does not raise Canadian GDP.

questions.prompt: Part (d): “The purchase of a new airliner by WestJet” is the purchase of a final good.
questions.explanation: The airliner is not used up in producing another good during the year; it is a **capital good** bought by its final user, counted as gross fixed capital formation.

questions.prompt: Transaction 1: You hire CPKC to pull a holiday-themed railcar across Canada to celebrate the end of the fall semester. Which component of GDP is affected?

options.text: Gross fixed capital formation
Net exports
Final consumption
None: it is an intermediate good/service

questions.explanation: You are a final user buying a service for your own enjoyment: **final consumption** (household purchase of a service).

questions.prompt: Transaction 2: CPKC buys new rail oil tanker cars from Procor in Oakville, ON. Which component of GDP is affected?

options.text: Final consumption
Net exports
None: it is an intermediate good/service
Gross fixed capital formation

questions.explanation: Tanker cars are durable equipment bought by a firm and used for many years: **gross fixed capital formation**.

questions.prompt: Transaction 3: CPKC buys new track signalling software from IBM. Which component of GDP is affected?

options.text: Gross fixed capital formation
Final consumption
Net exports
None: it is an intermediate good/service

questions.explanation: Software used over many years is a fixed asset: **gross fixed capital formation** (an intellectual-property investment).

questions.prompt: Transaction 4: CPKC purchases 1,000,000 litres of diesel fuel from the Co-op refinery in Regina, SK. Which component of GDP is affected?

options.text: Final consumption
None: it is an intermediate good/service
Gross fixed capital formation
Net exports

questions.explanation: Fuel is used up in producing rail service, so it is an **intermediate good**; its value is already inside the price of the final service. It affects no component directly.

source.note: Textbook gives no key; answer follows the intended reading that shipping goods to the US is an export of transportation services.

questions.prompt: Transaction 5: CPKC takes railcars full of EV batteries from plants in Ontario to Detroit, Michigan. Which component of GDP is affected?

options.text: Final consumption
Gross fixed capital formation
Net exports
None: it is an intermediate good/service

questions.explanation: The service is delivered to a destination in the United States for export: the sale of rail transportation services to a foreign market is an **export**, which raises **net exports**. (If the shipper were instead an intermediate input to the battery maker, its value would already be in the price of the exported batteries; either way the output is counted through net exports, not consumption or investment.)

questions.prompt: Transaction 6: The Ontario government builds a new highway to improve access to the CPKC intermodal terminal in Vaughan, ON. Which component of GDP is affected?

options.text: Final consumption
Net exports
None: it is an intermediate good/service
Gross fixed capital formation

questions.explanation: A highway is a long-lived fixed asset purchased by government: **gross fixed capital formation** (the government-investment part of G in Y = C + I + G + Nx).

questions.prompt: The value of a house built in 2014 and resold in 2026 is included in the GDP of 2026.
questions.explanation: GDP counts only goods **produced** during the period. The house was produced in 2014 and counted in 2014 GDP; reselling it only transfers ownership. **Used goods are not counted again.**

questions.prompt: The services of the real estate agent who helped sell the house in 2026 are counted in the GDP of 2026.
questions.explanation: The agent’s services are **newly produced** in 2026 (a final service bought by the seller or buyer), so the commission is part of 2026 GDP even though the house itself is not.

questions.prompt: What is nominal GDP for 2027 (in dollars)?
questions.explanation: Cotton is an intermediate good (all of it goes into shirts), so exclude it. Nominal GDP = 100×$60 + 100×$2 + 50×$25 = 6,000 + 200 + 1,250 = **$7,450**. Including the cotton (80 × $0.60 = $48) would double count it.

questions.prompt: Do you agree with this statement? “In years when people buy many shares of stock, investment will be high and, therefore, so will GDP.”

options.text: Disagree: buying shares is a financial transaction that transfers ownership of existing claims; “investment” in GDP means purchases of new capital goods (fixed capital and inventories)
Agree: buying stock gives firms funds, and every dollar a firm receives is counted in GDP
Agree: stock purchases are a form of saving, and saving is a component of GDP
Disagree: stock purchases are counted in GDP only when the shares are newly issued

questions.explanation: In GDP, **investment means spending on newly produced physical capital** (and inventories). Buying shares is a financial investment that moves money between people; no new good or service is produced by the purchase itself. It therefore does **not** add to GDP. (The only link is indirect, if a firm uses the funds to buy new capital.)

questions.prompt: Why does cutting debt and increasing personal saving affect consumer spending?

options.text: Paying down debt automatically raises household income, so consumption must rise
Income used to pay down debt or to save is not available to spend, so consumption falls unless income rises
Saving is itself a form of consumption, so consumption is unchanged
Debt payments are counted in GDP, so cutting them lowers consumption

questions.explanation: Households divide disposable income between spending and saving/debt repayment. Each dollar devoted to **repaying debt or saving is a dollar not spent**, so consumer spending (the largest component of GDP) falls unless income grows.

questions.prompt: What would happen to GDP and incomes if the majority of consumers decided to reduce their spending at the same time?

options.text: GDP would fall but incomes would rise, since households would be saving more
GDP and incomes would not change, because saving is spent by banks automatically
GDP and incomes would fall, since one person’s spending is another person’s income (total spending = total income)
GDP would rise, because lower consumption makes room for more investment

questions.explanation: From the circular flow, **spending = production = income**. If most households cut spending, firms’ revenue falls, so they pay out less income, which leads to still less spending. Unless investment, government spending or net exports rise to offset it, **GDP and incomes fall**.

questions.prompt: For the value of expenditures on final goods to equal total income, all the money a business receives from selling its product must be paid out as income to the owners of the factors of production. How can a business make a profit if it pays out as income all the money it receives?

options.text: Profit is revenue that is kept by the firm and is therefore not part of income
Profit is paid to the government as taxes, which are not income
A firm can pay out all of its revenue only if its profit is zero
Profit is itself income: it is the part of revenue paid to the firm’s owners, so paying out all revenue includes paying out the profit

questions.explanation: Revenue is paid to **workers (wages), lenders (interest), landlords (rent) and the firm’s owners (profit)**. Profit is the residual income of the owners, so it is part of the total income paid out. Nothing is left over: the income approach to GDP includes profits as part of gross operating surplus.

questions.prompt: What was the total value added by the artist for the 10 sculptures (in dollars)?
questions.explanation: Artist’s revenue = 10 × $800 = $8,000. Intermediate goods = $5,000 of scrap metal. **Value added = 8,000 − 5,000 = $3,000.**

questions.prompt: What was the total value added by the local art store for the 10 sculptures (in dollars)?
questions.explanation: The store sells for 10 × $1,000 = $10,000 and pays $8,000 for the sculptures (its intermediate input). **Value added = 10,000 − 8,000 = $2,000.** Only the final $10,000 sale enters GDP; it equals the sum of value added at every stage (steel mill's part + $3,000 + $2,000).

questions.prompt: Why does the size of a country’s GDP matter? How does it affect the quality of life of its people?

options.text: A larger GDP (especially per person) means more goods and services are available, and more resources for health care, education and other things that improve living standards
A larger GDP guarantees that income is equally distributed among citizens
GDP size determines a country’s inflation rate, which sets its standard of living
It does not: GDP has no relationship to the quality of life

questions.explanation: Higher production per person means higher incomes and a greater ability to buy goods and services and to fund health care, education and environmental protection. Countries with higher real GDP per person generally have longer life expectancy and better living standards, though GDP does not guarantee equality or happiness.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are reasons why GDP is an imperfect measure of economic well-being? Select all that apply.

options.text: It excludes household production (e.g. unpaid childcare and cooking)
It counts intermediate goods several times
It excludes production in the informal economy
It includes the value of used goods when they are resold
It places no value on leisure time
It is not adjusted for pollution or crime

questions.explanation: GDP leaves out **household production** and the **informal economy**, and even a perfect production measure would not value **leisure**, pollution, crime and social problems, or the distribution of income. It does **not** double count intermediate goods or include used goods; the definition is built to avoid exactly those.

questions.prompt: The fraction of women working outside the home increases. Measured GDP is likely to increase.
questions.explanation: Work done outside the home is paid and recorded, and household services that used to be unpaid (cooking, childcare) are now often bought in the market. Measured GDP **rises** (even though total production may not have changed as much).

source.note: Textbook Problem 2.3(b) is open-ended; the reading used here is that GDP is not adjusted for crime, so security spending raises measured GDP while well-being falls. (Crime that drives people away from work or shopping could instead reduce activity.)

questions.prompt: There is a sharp increase in the crime rate. Because GDP counts the extra spending on police, alarms and security services but does not subtract the harm done by crime, measured GDP is likely to increase.
questions.explanation: Crime itself is not counted in GDP (and illegal trade is largely unmeasured), but the **response** is: more spending on police, locks, alarms and security services is final output that is counted. So measured GDP tends to rise even though well-being falls, which illustrates that GDP is not adjusted for crime.

questions.prompt: Higher tax rates cause some people to hide more of the income they earn. Measured GDP is likely to increase.
questions.explanation: Income and production that people hide moves into the **informal economy**, which GDP does not capture. Measured GDP therefore **falls** (though actual production may be unchanged).

questions.prompt: The typical Canadian works fewer than 40 hours a week today, versus about 60 hours in 1890. What does this tell us about economic well-being today compared with 1890?

options.text: Well-being is lower today, because fewer hours worked means less production
Well-being is very likely higher today: real GDP per person is much greater and there is more leisure time, which GDP does not count, so GDP per person alone understates the improvement
Hours worked tell us nothing; real GDP per person is a complete measure of well-being
Well-being cannot be compared because the price level has changed since 1890

questions.explanation: GDP does not value **leisure**. Canadians today enjoy far higher real GDP per person *and* more leisure than in 1890, so the real improvement in well-being is **larger** than the GDP comparison alone suggests. Fewer hours do not mean lower well-being, and GDP per person is not a complete measure (real GDP already adjusts for price changes).

questions.prompt: Which country has the highest GNI per person?

options.text: Norway
United Arab Emirates
Singapore
United States

questions.explanation: Ranking by GNI per person: Singapore (88,761), UAE (74,104), Norway (69,190), US (65,565), Austria, Canada, South Korea, Greece, China, Iran, Venezuela, Zimbabwe.

questions.prompt: Which country has the highest HDI?

options.text: Singapore
Canada
United Arab Emirates
Norway

questions.explanation: Ranking by HDI: Norway (0.966), Singapore (0.949), UAE (0.937), Canada (0.935), South Korea (0.929), US (0.927), Austria (0.926), Greece, China, Iran, Venezuela, Zimbabwe. Norway tops HDI although Singapore is richer in GNI per person.

questions.prompt: What is Canada’s rank (1 = highest) in the HDI list?
questions.explanation: HDI order: Norway, Singapore, UAE, **Canada (4th)**. In the GNI-per-person list Canada is 6th, so it ranks two places higher on HDI.

questions.prompt: Which best explains why the two rankings differ?

options.text: HDI also includes life expectancy and education, so countries with long lives and high schooling rank relatively higher on HDI than their income alone suggests, and vice versa
HDI is calculated from nominal GDP, whereas GNI is calculated from real GDP
GNI per person ignores income earned abroad, whereas HDI includes it
HDI measures income inequality only, so it differs from GNI

questions.explanation: GNI per person measures **income only**. HDI adds **health and education** components, so a country’s HDI rank can differ from its income rank. For example, the US is 4th on GNI but 6th on HDI, and Canada is 6th on GNI but 4th on HDI. HDI is a broader measure of well-being.

questions.prompt: Which element of the expenditure approach is likely to change the most when illicit cannabis is included?

options.text: Net exports
Final consumption (household purchases of cannabis)
Gross fixed capital formation
Investment in inventories

questions.explanation: Cannabis is bought mostly by households for their own use, so it shows up in **final consumption**. The other categories are little affected.

source.note: Open-ended in the text; illicit growers and dealers are mostly unincorporated, so gross mixed income (and gross operating surplus) change most.

questions.prompt: Which element(s) of the income approach are likely to change the most when illicit cannabis is included?

options.text: Compensation of employees only
Taxes less subsidies only
Gross mixed income and gross operating surplus (the earnings of growers and sellers)
Statistical discrepancy only

questions.explanation: Illicit growers and dealers are mostly self-employed or unincorporated owners earning **gross mixed income** and profits (**gross operating surplus**). Little of it is formal wages or taxes before legalization.

source.note: Open-ended in the text; the answer given is the standard reading (government-run stores add employee pay, operating surplus and sales taxes, and displace some mixed income).

questions.prompt: Which income-approach items are most likely to change due to government-run cannabis stores (Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, PEI)?

options.text: Gross mixed income only, which rises
Final consumption and net exports
No component changes, since the same cannabis is sold
Compensation of employees and gross operating surplus / taxes less subsidies of the government-run stores, replacing some mixed income

questions.explanation: Government-run stores hire employees (**compensation of employees**) and earn a profit for government (**operating surplus**, plus taxes on sales), while unregistered sellers’ **mixed income** shrinks. Total spending on cannabis may be similar, but the income is distributed across different categories.

questions.prompt: In what sense does GDP offer a summary statistic of how well an economy is doing?

options.text: It adds up the market value of all final production into one number that equals total income, so higher GDP generally means more goods and services and more income
It measures every activity that contributes to human well-being
It measures the distribution of income across households
It measures only the quantity of goods, not their prices

questions.explanation: One number captures the economy’s total output and, by the circular-flow identity, its total income. Growth in real GDP signals more production, jobs and income.

questions.prompt: Why does the author add the words “or seems to”?

options.text: Because GDP is always measured with large errors that cannot be corrected
Because GDP leaves out household production, the informal economy, leisure, pollution, crime and income distribution, so it is not a complete measure of well-being
Because GDP does not include government spending
Because GDP is not calculated with the expenditure approach

questions.explanation: The qualification reflects the **limits of GDP**: nonmarket activity, leisure, environmental damage, crime and inequality are not captured.

questions.prompt: Why does inflation make nominal GDP a poor measure of the increase in total production from one year to the next? How does Statistics Canada deal with this?

options.text: Inflation makes nominal GDP fall; Statistics Canada therefore adds the inflation rate back
Inflation reduces output; Statistics Canada therefore uses only the value of intermediate goods
Nominal GDP rises when prices rise even if output does not; Statistics Canada calculates real GDP using constant (base-year) prices so that changes reflect only quantities
Nominal GDP ignores prices altogether; Statistics Canada therefore uses current prices instead

questions.explanation: Nominal GDP = current prices × current quantities, so it can grow purely because prices rose. **Real GDP** values each year’s output at **constant base-year prices**, so its changes reflect changes in quantities produced. (Statistics Canada actually uses chain-weighted prices to reduce distortion.)

questions.prompt: What is the GDP deflator, and how is it calculated?

options.text: A measure of total output: real GDP divided by nominal GDP, times 100
A measure of the inflation rate: the change in nominal GDP divided by the change in real GDP
A measure of the price of consumer goods only: consumer spending divided by population
A measure of the price level: nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100

questions.explanation: GDP deflator = **(Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100**. It is a price-level measure covering all final goods; its percentage change between years is the inflation rate measured by the deflator.

questions.prompt: In the years after the base year:

options.text: Nominal GDP is greater than real GDP
Nominal GDP equals real GDP
Nominal GDP is less than real GDP
The relationship cannot be determined

questions.explanation: Prices are higher than base-year prices, so valuing output at current prices gives a bigger number: **nominal > real**.

questions.prompt: In the base year:

options.text: Nominal GDP is greater than real GDP
Nominal GDP equals real GDP
Nominal GDP is less than real GDP
The relationship cannot be determined

questions.explanation: Current prices are the base-year prices, so **nominal = real** (and the deflator = 100).

questions.prompt: In the years before the base year:

options.text: Nominal GDP is greater than real GDP
Nominal GDP equals real GDP
Nominal GDP is less than real GDP
The relationship cannot be determined

questions.explanation: Prices were lower than base-year prices, so **nominal < real** (deflator below 100).

source.note: The table’s cotton quantity of 800 in 2018 looks like a misprint, but cotton is excluded from GDP so it does not affect the answer.

questions.prompt: What is real GDP for 2018 (in 2009 dollars)?
What is real GDP for 2019 (in 2009 dollars)?
What is the growth rate of real GDP during 2019 (in percent, one decimal)?
I agree with: “If nominal GDP is less than real GDP, then the price level must have fallen during the year.”
questions.explanation: Nominal < real only says that prices are **below their base-year level** (the year is before the base year). Prices may well have risen from the previous year. **Disagree.**

questions.prompt: I agree with: “Whenever real GDP declines, nominal GDP must also decline.”
questions.explanation: Nominal GDP = P × Q. If prices rise by more than real output falls, nominal GDP can still rise. **Disagree.**

questions.prompt: I agree with: “If a recession is so severe that the price level declines, then we know that both real GDP and nominal GDP must decline.”
questions.explanation: A recession means real GDP falls. If the price level also falls, nominal GDP (price × quantity) falls too, since both factors decline. **Agree.**

questions.prompt: I agree with: “Nominal GDP declined between 2018 and 2019; therefore, the GDP deflator must also have declined.”
questions.explanation: Nominal GDP can fall because real GDP fell while prices rose (or fell by less). The deflator = nominal ÷ real × 100 depends on both. **Disagree.**

questions.prompt: One of the textbook authors argues that rising oil prices are likely to be neutral for Canada’s real GDP but will definitely raise nominal GDP. Can we tell what effect higher oil prices are expected to have on the inflation rate?

options.text: No: inflation depends on real GDP only, which is unchanged
Yes: inflation falls, because higher oil prices reduce households’ real incomes
No: nominal GDP and real GDP never tell us anything about the price level
Yes: nominal GDP rises while real GDP does not, so the GDP deflator (price level) rises, which means higher inflation

questions.explanation: Deflator = (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100. If nominal GDP rises and real GDP stays the same, the **deflator rises**: the price level goes up, so the **inflation rate is higher**.

questions.prompt: (a) Real GDP for 2014 with base year 2016?
(a) Real GDP for 2017 with base year 2016?
(a) Real GDP for 2014 with base year 2018?
(a) Real GDP for 2017 with base year 2018?

What effect does changing the base year have on the calculated percentage changes in real GDP?

options.text: Very little: the levels of real GDP change, but the growth rates are nearly the same (only small differences from the different relative price weights)
It changes the sign of the growth rates, since a different year’s prices are used
It has no effect on the level of real GDP but a large effect on growth rates

questions.explanation: Moving the base year rescales the **levels** of real GDP (1,088.9 vs 1,198.0 in 2014), but growth rates barely change (−5.29% vs −5.33%). The differences are small because the two deflator series move almost in proportion.

questions.prompt: An article says “the euro zone’s GDP grew at an annualized rate of around 2 percent in the first quarter.” Is it likely referring to nominal or real GDP growth?

options.text: Nominal GDP: only nominal GDP can be measured quarterly
Real GDP: news reports of economic growth refer to the increase in actual production, with price changes removed
Nominal GDP: real GDP can never grow as slowly as 2 percent
Neither: GDP growth is always expressed as the inflation rate

questions.explanation: Growth of the economy means **more goods and services**, which is measured by **real GDP** growth. Nominal GDP growth would mix in inflation, so it is not the standard way to report how fast the economy is growing.

questions.explanation: Percentage changes in the deflator: 2013 = 1.62%, **2014 = 1.79%**, 2015 = 1.08%, 2016 = 1.31%. So 2014 had the largest increase in the price level.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between GDP and GNI?

options.text: GDP includes depreciation, GNI includes only net investment
GDP is the expenditure measure and GNI is the income measure of the same domestic production
GDP excludes government spending, GNI includes it
GDP values production within a country’s borders; GNI measures the income received by the country’s residents for the use of their factors of production, wherever that production occurs

questions.explanation: GDP = where production happens; **GNI = who earns the income** (GDP + income received from abroad − income paid abroad). Both include depreciation.

questions.prompt: Is the difference between GDP and GNI important for Canada?

options.text: No: for Canada the difference is small, because incomes earned abroad by Canadians and incomes earned in Canada by foreigners are similar in size
Yes: Canada’s GNI is more than double its GDP
Yes: Canada’s GDP is much larger than GNI because foreign firms own most Canadian capital
No: GNI and GDP are always exactly equal in every country

questions.explanation: Canadian GDP and GNI are close in value (GNI is slightly below GDP because of net investment income paid abroad), so the difference is small relative to GDP, unlike, say, Ireland where GDP is about 20% larger than GNI.

questions.prompt: What are the differences between national income, household income and household disposable income?

options.text: National income = GDP plus transfers; household income = GNI minus taxes; disposable income = household income plus saving

National income = GNI minus depreciation (consumption of fixed capital); household income = income received by households, including transfers but excluding firms’ retained earnings; disposable income = household income minus personal taxes
National income is the income of households; household income is the income of firms; disposable income is after-tax profit
All three are the same thing measured at different times of the year

questions.explanation: National (net national) income subtracts **depreciation** from GNI. Household income adds transfer payments and leaves out retained earnings. **Household disposable income = household income − personal tax payments**, the income households actually have available to spend.

questions.prompt: What is gross domestic income?

options.text: The sum of household disposable income and government spending
The value of all final goods bought by households
The total of all incomes earned from domestic production: compensation of employees, gross operating surplus, gross mixed income and taxes less subsidies (plus a statistical discrepancy)
The income of Canadians from all sources, including from abroad

questions.explanation: Gross domestic income is the income-approach total, equal to GDP up to the statistical discrepancy. It is **domestic** (earned in Canada), unlike GNI.

questions.prompt: Which component of gross domestic income is the largest?

options.text: Gross operating surplus
Gross mixed income
Taxes less subsidies
Compensation of employees

questions.explanation: Compensation of employees (wages, salaries and employer contributions) is about **51%** of GDP, followed by gross operating surplus (≈26%), gross mixed income (≈13%) and taxes less subsidies (≈10%).

questions.prompt: A country has many citizens temporarily working in other countries and many firms with facilities abroad, while relatively few foreign citizens or foreign firms operate in the country. Which would you expect to be larger, GDP or GNI?

options.text: GNI, because income earned abroad by its residents and firms exceeds the income earned domestically by foreigners
GDP, because production abroad is counted in domestic production
They would be equal, because GDP always equals GNI
GDP, because foreign production inside the country is large

questions.explanation: GNI = GDP + income earned by the country’s residents abroad − income earned by foreigners at home. Here the first term is large and the second small, so **GNI > GDP**.

questions.prompt: Ireland’s GDP is about 20 percent larger than its GNI, so Irish people “appear (when using GDP per person) to be richer than what they feel they are.” Explain the author’s reasoning.

options.text: Ireland’s GDP double counts intermediate goods, while GNI does not

Much of the production in Ireland is by foreign-owned multinationals, and their profits flow abroad to foreign owners, so the income actually received by Irish residents (GNI) is smaller than domestic production (GDP)
The Irish government’s taxes are included in GNI but not in GDP
GDP per person ignores Irish citizens who work abroad, whereas GNI counts foreigners working in Ireland

questions.explanation: GDP counts all production in Ireland, including that of foreign firms. Their profits are income to foreigners and are not part of Irish GNI. GNI per person thus gives a truer picture of Irish incomes than GDP per person.

questions.prompt: The federal government collects more personal income tax while GDP stays the same. What happens to national income, household income and household disposable income?

options.text: All three fall
National income falls; household income and disposable income are unchanged
National income and household income are unchanged; household disposable income falls
Household income rises; national income and disposable income are unchanged

questions.explanation: Household disposable income = household income − personal taxes, so it **falls**. National income depends on production (GDP), which is unchanged. Household income is measured before personal taxes, so it too is unchanged.

questions.prompt: To forecast household consumption spending, which measure of total production or income would be most helpful?

options.text: GDP
Gross national income
National income
Household disposable income

questions.explanation: Households can spend only what they have after paying personal taxes, so **household disposable income** is the best predictor of consumption spending.
